Here’s the Real Problem With Stock Buybacks
 
Plus, 40 trillion reasons to worry
 

Sure, it’s just a number, but it’s a really, really big one. America’s national debt topped $40 trillion on the same day that the U.S. Treasury announced plans to buy back more long-term bonds, sending their yields lower. That’ll be paid for with other borrowing, of course. Oil prices are higher again and, after a rebound yesterday, stock futures point to a muted U.S. open.

Sell high, buy lower

 

Warren Buffett is normally courteous, but he had some choice words for critics of stock buybacks a few years ago.

 

“When you are told that all repurchases are harmful to shareholders or to the country, or particularly beneficial to CEOs, you are listening to either an economic illiterate or a silver-tongued demagogue (characters that are not mutually exclusive),” he wrote.

 

Note Buffett’s emphasis on the word “all.” Companies need to return cash to investors eventually to be worth owning. For the most part, the differences between doing that via dividends or buybacks are minor.

 

Buybacks give long-term investors a larger stake in a smaller company instead of handing them cash they may not need and a dividend tax bill they definitely don’t. For management, dividends create future expectations whereas buybacks can be turned on and off.

 

But buybacks aren’t always a good idea because sometimes stocks are expensive. Companies that grant lots of stock options can be indifferent because they want to soak up those cheaply issued shares. Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway, which doesn’t pay dividends, also suspended buybacks for nearly two years, amassing a record cash hoard.

 

Red-hot chip maker SK Hynix’s announcement Wednesday that it would conduct South Korea’s largest-ever buyback sent its shares higher. It’s a head-scratcher, though. 

 

Even after a recent slump, the stock was up 470% from a year earlier. Management had ample financial firepower to buy during that ascent and didn’t. Even weirder is that they sold nearly the same amount of stock to U.S. investors just last month in the biggest share sale ever by a foreign company at an effective price 50% higher than today.

 

At least SK Hynix sold high and is buying lower. U.S. companies often get that backward.

 

For example, S&P 500 members marked what was then a record for buybacks in the same quarter the dot-com bubble peaked. The effective buyback yield—the value of repurchases as a ratio of the S&P 500’s value—was just 1.2%. Three years later, they spent about 40% less, yet the yield was a third higher.

 

The contrast was even more extreme during the financial crisis. Buybacks hit a record just as stocks did in 2007. By the spring of 2009, when the market was dirt cheap, buybacks had dropped by 85%.

 

Buybacks aren’t accounting trickery, and they don’t starve companies of capital unless done recklessly. The share of corporate profits returned to investors one way or another has been pretty steady over many decades.

 

But paying a dividend, reducing debt or building up cash for a rainy day can be better choices sometimes. Executives can’t control the business cycle or share prices. They’re in the best position to know when they’re frothy, though, and don’t always act like it.
